title: 2023 Study Abroad Experience at the Medical University of Vienna
paragraphs: I am very glad to have been able to take part in this exchange program, which was realized through the efforts of the professors and has been handed down by my seniors. For two months, from March 6 to April 28, 2023, I was allowed to do clerkships at the hospital of the Medical University of Vienna in Vienna, the capital of Austria.

The hospital of the Medical University of Vienna is called AKH (Allgemeines Krankenhaus: general hospital) locally, is not far from the city center crowded with tourist sights such as the Opera House and the Imperial Palace, and is proud to be the largest hospital among Austria's four public medical schools. It was established in 1365, in the era of the Holy Roman Empire, as the medical faculty within the University of Vienna, and I understand it separated in 2004 as the Medical University of Vienna and has continued to the present. For that reason its campus is close to that of the University of Vienna, and during my study abroad I also went several times to social gatherings held by University of Vienna students. In particular, at the Vienna Wednesday language exchange meeting hosted by students of the Japanese language department, I made friends with several people and heard various stories about their home countries and hobbies. Near the university there is a medical museum called the Josephinum, named after Joseph II, son of Maria Theresa of the Habsburgs, where numerous wax anatomical models made in the 18th century for medical education and the history of medicine in Austria are exhibited, and it was interesting to be able to touch the efforts of those who came before and the development of medicine through the era of war. The Medical University of Vienna is also the university where the surgeon Billroth, famous for the Billroth method of gastrectomy, once served as professor of surgery, and which produced Landsteiner, who discovered the ABO blood groups and won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, so it is a university active in both research and clinical practice. Connected directly to a station on subway line 6, with a large 21-story ward building, 1,732 beds, about 50 operating rooms and about 600 students per year, a hospital much more concentrated than in Japan and of a scale beyond my imagination was very stimulating.
At the Medical University of Vienna I was allowed to do clerkships in three departments: cardiac surgery, thoracic surgery and radiology.

- Radiology: I did my clerkship in radiology for the latter four weeks. What surprised me first was the large scale. There were many rooms across three floors, the 6th to 8th floors, for examinations, image reading and IVR, and about 100 radiologists worked there. The divisions were finely divided; for example, even within the CT reading rooms they were divided into surgical, medical, emergency and neurological. Every day, with a different room and a different doctor, I could see various cases, such as chest X-ray reading, abdominal MRI reading, PET-CT reading, ultrasound examinations and biopsies of the liver and kidney, and there were also opportunities to discuss the location of lesions together with the doctors. The radiology doctors were very kind, and many were enthusiastic about teaching, and I was able to spend a fulfilling four weeks. There were also many opportunities to talk slowly with the doctors, and I was happy that there were more people than expected who were interested in Japan and had a good impression of it. Hearing from doctors who had spent their residency in other countries such as London and Paris, I felt the way of working across countries that is unique to Europe.

Apart from the above clerkships at the Medical University of Vienna, I also met a doctor from Nagoya University who works at a community hospital in Vienna and was able to observe the community hospital once. The doctor looked after me a great deal, and I listened with great interest to his career and stories. In addition, I had the opportunity to receive echo training from a doctor who is an acquaintance of that doctor, who graduated from the Medical University of Vienna and now works at another university hospital in Austria, which was very instructive. Thank you.

The city of Vienna was a wonderful city full of sights. Statues of famous musicians such as Beethoven and Mozart stand in various places in the city, and being able to enjoy wonderful music at standing-room seats at the Opera House and the Musikverein at not-high prices was a happy experience for me. The house where Mozart lived with his family and the house where Beethoven recuperated have become museums, and I could imagine under what circumstances the musicians composed their works. The beautiful museums displaying paintings by Austrian artists such as Klimt and Egon Schiele, and the delicious coffee and the great variety of wines were also attractive.

What I felt throughout the two months is that at the Medical University of Vienna, where there are many medical staff and many exchange students come and go, it is almost impossible to keep track of when and which exchange students come. In the operating room, I had to introduce myself every time to all the staff involved in the operation as an exchange student from Japan and tell them that I wanted to scrub into or observe the operation. The local students always did this too. Thanks to that, I felt the clerkships went smoothly, and I understood and realized that, even amid anxiety and much that I did not understand, my own attitude of speaking up actively opens up chances.

Finally, with many concerns in the background because of the spread of the coronavirus, I would like to thank everyone at the International Collaboration Office, starting with Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川, Dr. Itzel and Dr. Branko, who arranged this valuable opportunity, the doctors who instructed us in the pre-departure training, the people at the Medical University of Vienna who accepted me, and everyone who looked after me on site. Making use of this experience, I intend to continue making efforts so that I can become a doctor who contributes to patients and to healthcare.
